title: APIO 2026 Reflection
content: My reflection on APIO 2026. Global Rank: 79, Region Rank: 4, Points: 68.66, Medal: Bronze, Performance: Extremely Bad. APIO 2026 ReflectionOverviewSince Mainland China team didn’t participate (probably bc it was held in tw) and held its own APIO with different problems, I guess this year’s cutoffs will be easier? Rank Worldwide: Medal: Bronze Rank in HK: (Finally enter top !!!) Score: Performance: Extremely Bad No. Difficulty Expected Reality 1 NOI/NOI+/CTSC 2 NOI/NOI+/CTSC 3 省选/NOI- Pre-competitionDid some APIO past paper. APIO 2025: , easy silver. Gold is too hard. Hopefully, APIO 2026 silver? I went to F/ and it was a parking lot. Then I went to /F and ethening told us it was wrong??? Darn. TimelineVery inaccurate timeline. - mins: Reading problems Why are APIO problems so difficult to read??? last year’s wasn’t like this, maybe it was because I used luogu with simplified Chinese NO IDEA WHATSOEVER. And, I read T3 for like times and still don’t understand it. Maybe because I read it too fast. Darn. - mins: What did I do? IDK. Switching between P1 and P2 thinking full sol. P1 similar to T251? Nah it’s coincidence. I realize P1 is not so simple. I quickly realized that this year’s difficulty is probably black black black. Oh no. Here are my thoughts: My first thoughts on P1 is you must get rid of nodes with no use (already satisfied). Then some sort of DP? But I can’t DP. Then P2, I want to just assign each edge to but it doesn’t work. I should also incorporate depth data. Actually I just need depth . Just need in Subtask , . Easy pts get. Back to P1. I realize the optimal solution is probably to start at a node and take a prefix of some euler tour. But IDK. Write Subtask first. pts :((( Back to P2. After thinking for a long time, I realize the solution is almost unique in chains. The method is extremely creative: observe that the cycles , , takes colors and . So you just fill each segment with the cycles and you are done. Get pts, nice. Wait why is there only hours left??? Back to P1. I write Subtask and after some debugging get pts. Back to P2. I only got pts in Subtask , so aim pts (I don’t think I ever aimed for pts in my entire life, this is first time bro). It was quite easy so I get it in reasonable time. But wait, what about P3? In total, I think I spent around mins on P3, which is way less than average time per problem. Mostly because I thought it was hardest problem in the problemset (big mistake!). And at the end I didn’t even understand it. I really have to improve my comprehension skills! After the problems were posted on Codeforces, I read it out loud and finally understood the problem statement :( ReflectionIn conclusion, the reason why I failed this competition is completely because of P3, which I never thought might be case during the competition. It turns out a lot of people ACed P3 (source: codeforces), including Adam :((( And I think I would’ve had a chance if I actually continued reading the statement. Even if I didn’t get AC, I would’ve probably got some subtasks, since both Andy and happyboy got reasonable scores in P3. On the other hand, I found that my P2 scores was very high in contestants (probably because I spent a lot of time on it and my constructive skills improved)! And my P1 is also pretty decent. Next time, especially in TFT, I must carefully read the problem statements of ALL problems and try to understand it! Sorry if this reflection really looks like a beginner’s reflection, but maybe I’m just too bad at APIO. THE END

content: A few problems from Codeforces that I think are both interesting and hard. Original: Chinese Translation: Gemini Codeforces TrainingLet’s start!Subset with Zero Sum A classic problem! Notice that the problem only requires finding any arbitrary construction, and observe that . Just connect the edges and find a cycle. Museums Tour Create a vertex for each . Construct the graph directly, condense it into SCCs, and run the longest path algorithm. However, there might be a scenario where visiting a museum on different days leads to double counting. But since repeating the same path times will return you to the original day, these two nodes must belong to the same SCC. Just use a map to store them. Got hacked awa. Coin Troubles Construct a graph; it must be a collection of cycles/chains. If there is a cycle, output . Otherwise, apply prefix sums to eliminate the partial order constraints, and then run a knapsack DP. Capitalism Graph construction. If it is not a bipartite graph, a contradiction arises due to parity. If there is a negative cycle, it’s definitely impossible. Otherwise, it behaves like a system of difference constraints; directly enumerate the minimum point, and run the shortest path algorithm to determine the maximum weight for each vertex (since it’s a bipartite graph, edges won’t become ). Use Floyd-Warshall for multi-source shortest path pre-processing. Multiple of Three Cycles An absolute god-tier problem! First, consider how to calculate the answer. Cycles can be removed directly, so focus on the remaining chains. Define the state as the answer when there are currently chains with lengths congruent to modulo , respectively. Then you realize is useless and can be computed directly. The problem reduces to finding , representing the answer when there are currently chains with lengths congruent to modulo . A direct DP takes , which is unfeasible. By writing down the algebraic equations, we find that for , knowing any two allows computing the third; similarly for . If we maintain and , we can transition to and . Work backward from the last valid state. For each query, the two coefficients of clearly increase monotonically, so we can just transition using brute force. The complexity is linear. Orac and Medians Thinking process: If already has adjacent identical elements, we are done. If there is a number greater than or equal to next to a , we are also done (note that “median” here is not the conventional median). Let’s denote “large” as and “small” as . What if is surrounded by small elements, but there are large elements further away? We find that as long as the large elements can overwrite the small elements, it works. We only need the large elements to become adjacent. In fact, we only need at least two large elements within any consecutive three elements. Conversely, if the distance between any two large elements is always , there is clearly no solution. Check this condition, and remember to handle the special case . Guess Divisors Count Guessing directly can rule out the case where . Otherwise, must be very large. Assuming we already know , we can only guess , so we must satisfy . Consider how to avoid . You realize that you need to query all primes from to . For primes , you need to query their first power greater than . For primes , you only need to query the prime itself. Multiplying multiple primes together to query allows completing it within queries. Chess Strikes Back Clearly binary search. Each grid must contain exactly one piece. We observe that the pieces placed in the top-left and those in the bottom-right must be separated by a path running from bottom-left to top-right. This is equivalent to saying there cannot exist such that and (where is the set of top-left placements and is the bottom-right set). Maintain this using any standard method. The rating is honestly inflated. Removing Leaves Consider arbitrarily designating any vertex that is not deleted at the end as the root. Tree DP is straightforward, then use rerooting. New Game with a Chess Piece Just find the pattern by printing a game matrix. Watch out for special cases. Stoned Game This seems to share an identical conclusion with about other problems. If a single pile contains more than half of the total stones, the first player wins unconditionally. Otherwise, understanding it intuitively or rigorously leads to the same result: you only need to check the parity. Divide Square Nice problem. Don’t miss the condition like I did: all segments are connected. Since the number of connected components is , we can directly apply Euler’s planar graph formula. By breaking down the contributions of (number of edges) into each intersection point, we reach the conclusion: the answer is the number of intersection points + the number of segments traversing the entire plane + 1. Solve using a scanning line. Reverse and Swap Why is this rated ? Is the data structure skill of international contestants really that bad… Just use a Segment Tree and maintain some tags. While writing, I realized that a reverse can be decomposed into two swaps, which successfully simplified the code. Fixed Point Removal Excellent problem; I overcomplicated it at first. Consider how to solve a single query. If initially , we change it to . Each time, choose an element with and decrement the interval by . Consider multiple queries, which can be solved offline. Maintain a pointer moving from largest to smallest. Each time, pick an element with and decrement by . If no such element can be chosen, move the pointer forward and keep trying. Then, the query is simply the number of deleted elements when the pointer is moved to . Of course, this can also be solved online using a Persistent Segment Tree. Deleting Numbers Nice problem. Clearly, is roughly the number of primes . Suppose we first use operations to delete all elements except the target number, then we could just query each prime one more time. However, this would take queries. For primes , we can directly apply the process mentioned above. For primes , the target number can have at most one of them as a factor. Thus, we can apply divide and conquer: test the first half of the primes first, then query if any of its factors are in this first half. If so, we only need to test the first half again and can discard the second half. If not, we recurse on the second half. The number of queries is approximately . Book Sorting An ICPC problem, great problem!! My Solution. Sketch: Guess an obvious conclusion, and then notice that the formula satisfies decision monotonicity, which allows us to maintain it using Mo’s algorithm. Fair Share Connect edges between set indices and element values. Choosing an equal amount is equivalent to the out-degree of the set being equal to its in-degree. Elements appearing an equal number of times is equivalent to the out-degree of the element being equal to its in-degree. Just find an Eulerian circuit. Flip and Reverse An absolute god-tier problem. For this kind of mysterious problem, consider graph construction: represents connecting from the current to and decrementing by , while represents connecting from the current to and incrementing by . The operation is equivalent to reversing the direction of a cycle. Directly find the lexicographically smallest Eulerian path (greedily). Switch and Flip Clearly, decompose into permutation cycles. Playing around with it reveals that a single permutation cycle requires at least operations, which is not ideal. Consider two permutation cycles; playing around with them reveals an ingenious method to resolve both simultaneously. If there is only one permutation cycle left at the end, just wrap it using the original method. Xor of 3 I overcomplicated this. If or , it is relatively simple and can be derived directly. Otherwise, find the first index such that , and push backward to , then resolve it using the method for . If no such exists where , there is no solution. Magnets Each time query , and notice that it will output a non-zero result upon reaching the second magnetic magnet. Suppose its index is . Then, for each , directly query to identify the subsequent magnetic magnets. The first magnetic magnet can be found by binary searching and querying . Dynamic Diameter Nice problem! My Solution. Sketch: Using the Euler Tour sequence, directly maintain the of the current node with a Segment Tree. Modifications correspond to interval additions on the subtrees’ Euler Tour segments, and queries look for on the Euler Tour sequence. This approach is useful for many problems regarding tree diameters (and of course, there is the important Diameter Merge Theorem). Sergey’s Problem God-tier problem. First, ignore the constraint that must not be adjacent, and greedily select elements in increasing order of their labels (i.e., do not select an element if the maximum distance constraint can be kept without it). At this stage, the maximum distance is at most . Now consider the pairs of vertices that are adjacent; we notice that these pairs form a DAG (since it can be easily proven that there are no cycles)!!! Run another greedy pass on this DAG in decreasing order of the labels. The maximum distance will then not exceed . Matrix Sorting Nice problem! Sorting is successful if and only if adjacent rows satisfy a partial order, which actually yields only conditions, instead of the conditions I initially thought. For each condition, we notice that the last sorting operation that affects the partial order relation of these adjacent rows must place them in correct order—this is the sole requirement. That is, the last sorting operation affecting these two rows cannot be in reverse order. Therefore, extract all sorting operations that have no constraints, execute them, and continuously update the constraints. This resembles a topological sort and can be implemented using a queue. Paint Notice that making the final color match either endpoint (e.g., the rightmost endpoint) is always optimal. Apply interval DP directly on it. Enumerate the last operation involving the rightmost endpoint; then can transition to and , provided that . In fact, if , then is obviously an invalid transition, i.e., suboptimal. Two Different Easy to get sidetracked. It is very easy to solve for lengths of . Thus, flatten the interval , and then flatten the interval . Clusterization Counting God-tier problem. Consider whether a set can form an independent cluster; this is equivalent to saying that all internal edges of are smaller than any edge connecting and . Consider adding edges in increasing order of their weights, then must form a clique within a connected component at some timestamp. Clearly, for any valid sets and , they are either completely disjoint or one contains the other, thereby forming a tree structure. Find this tree (which turns out to be the Kruskal Reconstruction Tree), and then each set forms a contiguous interval on the sequence. Finally, run a knapsack DP directly in the order of .

title: Dynamic Convex Hull
content: A simple Dynamic Convex Hull template that could solve a lot of difficult problems. Original: Chinese Translation: Gemini Took some insights from LineContainer implementation. Here, the meaning of p is the -coordinate where the current line loses its maximum status (becomes suboptimal). The meaning of the cmp function is to update u->p and return whether v has become obsolete (i.e., popped out of the convex hull). Key Points: Remember to handle the edge case where u.k == v.k. The behavior differs when maintaining an upper convex hull versus a lower convex hull. Remember to mark p as mutable, because multiset/set treats elements as const by default, making it impossible to update the value of p otherwise. Since multiset/set does not support random access queries, when querying , we cannot use ternary search. Instead, we should binary search the position of p using the container’s built-in lower_bound() function.
